extracted.intended_audience: architects, architecture students, and informed critics of historic and Gothic architecture
extracted.subtask_description: Guidelines and evaluative principles for designing and judging masonry arches, roof structures (roof proper vs roof mask), and roof cornices, with particular attention to Gothic and Venetian examples. Emphasises structural fitness, climatic appropriateness, and the placement of decoration.

rubrics_metrics.name: Dependence of arch safety on underlying masonry
rubrics_metrics.description: The safety, fitness, and beauty of ogee and all varieties of arch 'depends entirely for its safety, fitness, and beauty, on the masonry which we have just analysed.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Complex or richly varied arches may be beautiful but are structurally sound only when backed by properly designed masonry; on a large scale with many voussoirs such arches 'would be unsafe and absurd in general architecture.' Use such varieties occasionally for aesthetic effect, not as primary structural forms.

rubrics_metrics.name: Voussoir joint inclination and proportion
rubrics_metrics.description: The inclination of the joints of the voussoirs (their relation to the curve of the arch) is a matter of nicety; 'the natural idea' is that every voussoir should have the lengths of its outer and inner arched surface in the same proportion to each other.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Although not fully investigated by the author, this 'actual law, or a close approximation to it, is assuredly enforced in the best Gothic buildings.' Follow this proportional idea in cutting and shaping voussoirs for best results.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use decorative arch-forms sparingly
rubrics_metrics.description: Rich and fantastic varieties (e.g., ogee arches) admit exquisite beauty but should be used only occasionally.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Employ such forms for their decorative effect — they 'seem to stand by enchantment' — but avoid relying on them structurally at large scales; reserve them where their aesthetic charm outweighs structural complexity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Mixed-material substitution with proper backing
rubrics_metrics.description: Substituting marble side pieces with brick-filled spaces is permissible if the piece is 'properly backed by brickwork' and thus 'just as strong and safe a form' as the original.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: It is acceptable to combine materials (e.g., carving marble but filling with brick) provided the backing masonry is correctly designed to carry loads and ensure stability.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of cusps to counteract lateral thrust
rubrics_metrics.description: The use of the cusp in arches gives inward weight to large flank stones and 'prevent[s] their thrust outwards from being severely thrown on the lowermost stones.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Incorporate cusp elements where appropriate to add inward bearing and reduce outward thrust on critical stones; combine with discreet iron ties/bars where necessary to steady pillars.

rubrics_metrics.name: Iron ties to steady slender pillars
rubrics_metrics.description: In the example of the foursquare canopy at St. Anastasia, iron bars 'about an inch thick, connecting them at the heads of the abaci' are a feature of peculiar importance, steadying rather than materially assisting the pillars.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use iron ties/bars to steady slender supports where historic or structural context permits; treat them as stabilising elements rather than primary load-bearing members.

rubrics_metrics.name: Characterise arch load: loose vs massed
rubrics_metrics.description: Loads upon an arch may be perfectly loose (e.g., gravel or sand) or form one mass with the voussoirs (Mont-Cenisian); in practice the state is usually intermediate.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Design and analyse arches assuming the likely interaction between the arch and the overlying material: sometimes acting as dead weight, sometimes locking with the voussoirs and relieving pressure. Consider bridge/tunnel conditions versus architectural masonry when assessing loads.

rubrics_metrics.name: Filling intervals between arches to support roof
rubrics_metrics.description: To place a continuous roof above a line of arches, one must 'fill up the intervals between them on the tops of the columns' so as to obtain a level line of support.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Options include simple mass wall (roof laid on top) or introducing small secondary/vaulting shafts on top of the main shaft to convey roof weight to shaft heads and relieve arch centres. Choose arrangement based on desired distribution of loads and stylistic considerations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Arrangement and routing of secondary shafts
rubrics_metrics.description: A secondary shaft introduced to assist the roof may remain on the head of the great shaft, or be carried to the ground in front of it, or through it; when carried through, the main shaft divides into two or more minor shafts and forms a group.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The routing of vaulting shafts determines both structural behaviour and architectural principle: subordinate shafts (carried down the face or forming a small part of a group) imply Romanesque/Gothic principle, while a bold central shaft splitting the main pier suggests Classical/Palladian. Avoid arrangements that look superfluous (i.e., forms that could be removed 'without danger').

rubrics_metrics.name: Express the power of the arch clearly in form
rubrics_metrics.description: Some forms (e.g., Fig. XXXV form b) 'express the power of the arch most distinctly' and are described as purer and more sublime than arrangements resembling dovetailing or morticing of timber.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prefer arch forms that reveal structural logic and the arch's thrust and strength. Avoid stone arrangements that mimic timber joinery where they obscure the arch's character or create unsatisfactory capitals and supports.

rubrics_metrics.name: Careful management of capitals supporting vaulting shafts
rubrics_metrics.description: The author notes never having 'seen a single instance, quite satisfactory, of the management of the capital of the main shaft' when it has to sustain or allow passage of vaulting shafts.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Design capitals and brackets with attention to the loads they must sustain; do not rely on small brackets or decorative supports to carry portions of the roof that are structurally significant.

rubrics_metrics.name: Pierce spandrils to reduce weight without losing strength
rubrics_metrics.description: Triangular spaces (spandrils) on the flanks of the arch, if too heavy, 'may be diminished, while their strength remains the same, by piercing them with circular holes or lights.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use pierced spandrils where appropriate to reduce dead weight and add constructive and decorative value. This is particularly useful in bridges and iron roofs, and lends itself well to ornamentation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Distinguish Roof Proper from Roof Mask
rubrics_metrics.description: The roof generally has two divisions: the internally visible shell/vault/ceiling (the Roof Proper), whose business is strength, and an upper timber or other structure (the Roof Mask), whose purpose is to throw off snow and get rid of rain.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Treat the structural shell and the outer weather-protective mask as distinct design problems. Ensure the Roof Proper is structurally sound; design the Roof Mask primarily for weathering and climatic response.

rubrics_metrics.name: Limitations of lay critique on roof construction
rubrics_metrics.description: No person without long experience can tell whether a roof is wisely constructed or not; detailed internal examination is required.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid making authoritative judgments about roof structural quality based only on superficial observation; rely on expert inspection for Roof Proper assessments.

rubrics_metrics.name: Decorative roof outlines (domes, concave Chinese roofs) are mainly aesthetic
rubrics_metrics.description: Forms like eastern domes, cupolas, and the Chinese concave roof are 'purely decorative' and are of 'no more use, or rather of less, in throwing off snow or rain' than ordinary spires and gables.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use such outlines for aesthetic or picturesque effect and preferably on a small scale where their strangeness is desirable; do not choose them primarily for climatic effectiveness on large roofs.

rubrics_metrics.name: Gable with inward angle is often constructively right
rubrics_metrics.description: A gable with an inward angle (common in Germany/Switzerland) can act as an attached external pent-house or buttress and is 'often constructively right' and picturesque.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Consider inward-angled gables for protection of walls and as architectural buttressing; they can combine utility with strong picturesque effect.

rubrics_metrics.name: Match roof pitch and form to climate and habit
rubrics_metrics.description: The steep pitch of northern roofs arises from need to throw off snow, comfort of attic rooms in cold wet climates, and availability of timber; southern shallow slopes relate to different habits and climate.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Select roof pitch and form responsive to local climate, habitability of attic spaces, and available materials rather than symbolic or purely stylistic motives.

rubrics_metrics.name: Do not over-interpret symbolic intent in form
rubrics_metrics.description: Forms such as spires or steep gables have practical causes (climate, materials, habit) and are not necessarily intentional references to heaven or devotion.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Base historical and design explanations on practical and material conditions first; avoid attributing deep symbolic motives to functional forms without evidence.

rubrics_metrics.name: Provide buttresses for vaulting, not merely for roof mask
rubrics_metrics.description: As walls and roofs increase in height, 'it became more and more necessary to support them by buttresses;' however, 'it is not the steep roof mask which requires the buttress, but the vaulting beneath it.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Design buttresses principally to resist vaulting and internal thrusts; do not assume the external roof mask alone justifies heavy buttressing.

rubrics_metrics.name: Roof cornice should be designed for projection, not condensed weight
rubrics_metrics.description: The roof cornice is usually required 'rather to project boldly than to carry weight'; arrangements must secure the projection of large surfaces without being calculated to resist extraordinary pressure.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use brackets at intervals to support projection. Treat the cornice as the 'capital of the wall' in appearance but not necessarily in function; ensure supports are adequate for cantilevered projection rather than unexpected loads.

rubrics_metrics.name: Two families of roof cornices: eaved vs parapet/walk
rubrics_metrics.description: Roof cornices divide into: (1) eaved cornices composed merely by projection of the roof mask edge over the wall (sustained by brackets/spurs), and (2) cornices providing a walk round the edge of the roof, requiring stronger support and a parapet.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Choose the cornice family based on functional need: eaved for protection/shade and picturesque effect; parapet/walk cornices where circulation or defence (historically) is needed and heavier structural support is acceptable.

rubrics_metrics.name: Design of eaved cornice according to climate
rubrics_metrics.description: Eaved cornice is used in the north to throw rain away from walls, and in the south to give shade; ordinarily constructed of timber ends with tiles/shingles, sustained by spurs of timber.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: For northern climates emphasize projection and drainage; for southern climates use eaves for shading. Include interval waterspouts to avoid loading gutters at the edge with water weight.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prefer narrow stone cornice with stone gutter and small brackets for beauty and service
rubrics_metrics.description: When light is more valuable than shadow, drawing the cornice into narrower limits permits stone gutters supported by brackets, which may be delicately moulded; Venetian cornice praised as the most perfect and beautiful example.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: In contexts valuing light and visibility of wall ornament, prefer narrower stone cornices with stone gutters supported by small, moulded brackets; this offers simplicity and serviceableness.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid ornamenting the least visible surfaces
rubrics_metrics.description: It is a gross mistake in many cornices to charge ornament on the under surface of the cornice between brackets — 'the exact piece of the whole edifice... where ornament is least visible.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Place ornament where it will actually be seen by observers; do not reserve scarce decorative resources for surfaces not visible except from close vantage points.

rubrics_metrics.name: Maintain cornice integrity; do not fragment it onto shafts
rubrics_metrics.description: The architectural cornice is 'strictly and sternly limited to the end of the wall's speech—that is, to the edge of the roof' and 'has nothing whatever to do with shafts nor the orders of them.' Cutting the cornice to pieces and attaching bits to every column (a Renaissance error) is condemned.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Keep the cornice as a coherent horizontal element; avoid distributing fragments of it along shafts or columns merely because shafts travel through parts of the superstructure. Preservation of the cornice's visual and structural role is essential.

rubrics_metrics.name: Recognise two essential features of parapet cornices: bracket and parapet
rubrics_metrics.description: Parapet/walk cornices owe their form to military architecture and have two distinct features: (1) the bracket, of great practical service, and (2) the parapet.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When designing or evaluating such cornices, treat bracket design (for projection and support) and parapet design (for defence/walk) as primary considerations; learn the associated details of balconies and supports from these features.
